//: Lighthouse CI gate (PLAN §Loop 6a exit: Lighthouse ≥90; Loop 4b exit: TTI < 2.5 s
on mid-Android). Run with `make lighthouse`, or in CI via the `lighthouse` job.
`url` pins the audit to the app. Without it lhci audits every .html it finds in
the dist, and since 2026-09-01 the build stages every design page under docs/
into dist/docs/ (scripts/stage-docs.mjs) — documents, not the app, and not what
the ≥90 criterion is about. The port in that URL is replaced with the static
server's; the path is what matters.
Invoked as `pnpm dlx @lhci/cli autorun` — deliberately NOT a devDependency: it
pulls Lighthouse and a Chrome launcher (tens of MB) that nothing else in the repo
needs, and adding it would churn the shared lockfile for a tool that runs once
per push.
staticDistDir serves the built app the way Cloudflare Pages does (static files,
no server), which is the only deployment shape Hifth has. Hash routing means
index.html is the entire URL surface — every view is that one document plus
fetches, so one URL really is the whole app.
Several runs, median reported: a single headless run on a shared runner swings
several points on TBT alone, and a flaky gate is one people learn to re-run
instead of read. The count lives in `collect` below, with the measurements that
set it.
skipAudits: uses-http2 / canonical / is-crawlable are properties of the host and
of a public URL, neither of which a local static directory has; they are the
audits that would fail for the harness rather than the app. None of them carry
score weight in their categories.
THE DEVICE IS PINNED HERE, NOT INHERITED. Every number below is what
Lighthouse 12's mobile preset already used — a Moto G Power (2022) on Slow
4G with a 4× CPU slowdown — copied out of a report and written down. The
copying is the point: `interactive` is asserted below as Loop 4b's
*mid-Android* exit criterion, and if the profile is inherited then a
Lighthouse upgrade that retunes its default preset silently changes which
phone that criterion is about. A criterion whose device can move underneath
it is the same shape of gap as a criterion with no instrument.
So: pin it, and let a Lighthouse upgrade that disagrees show up as a diff
here rather than as a number that quietly means something else.
What this is NOT is a real phone. Throttling is `simulate` (Lantern): a fast
trace is collected and the slow device is modelled on top of it. The model
is far more host-independent than the hardware it runs on — 15 runs across
two machines whose benchmarkIndex spans 2142 to 3403 produced TTIs inside
2266–2437 ms, one cold CI run aside. That is why it is worth asserting.
It is still a model. backlog ② is the real-hardware check and stays open.
numberOfRuns is 5 rather than 3, and the reason is in the shape of those
measurements rather than in a preference for more data. Nine consecutive
local runs of one unchanged build came out bimodal — three at 2279–2284
and six at 2429–2437, with nothing in between. The gap is 150 ms, which is
`rttMs` above, to the millisecond: the LCP resource lands one simulated
round trip later in some runs than in others. So the metric does not
scatter, it steps, and a median has to be drawn from enough runs that one
step plus one cold start cannot carry it.
`interactive` is Loop 4b's exit criterion, and until now nothing evaluated
it. The four category assertions could not: in Lighthouse 12 the TTI audit
carries **weight 0** and sits in the `hidden` group, so a build can score a
perfect 100 on performance with a TTI of any size at all. ≥90 was never
making that promise, and reading it as if it were is the
interface-papering-over-a-gap failure this project has already paid for
twice.
Weight 0 is Lighthouse deprecating TTI in favour of TBT — which is a good
reason to distrust TTI as a *score*, and no reason at all to leave the exit
criterion unmeasured. The criterion says 2.5 s to interactive; this asserts
2.5 s to interactive. If a future Lighthouse removes the audit outright,
that is the moment to restate the criterion in TBT and LCP, and the upgrade
will say so rather than going quiet: renaming this key to an id Lighthouse
does not have was run, and lhci fails with `"…" is not a known audit` and
exit 1. A disappearing metric cannot turn this into a green no-op.
aggregationMethod is pinned rather than defaulted for the same reason the
device is. One of the three CI runs measured for this change came in at
2794 ms with 403 ms of blocking time while its two siblings agreed on
2283 ms — a cold runner, not a regression. A gate that fails on that is a
gate people re-run instead of read, which is the reasoning numberOfRuns
was already chosen for; the median is what makes that reasoning bite.
That was one observation when it was written, and it is now a pattern:
each of the two five-run sets since has contained exactly one such sample
— 2768 and 2806 — and in both sets it is the only run with any blocking
time at all, on the runner with the lowest benchmarkIndex of the five. One
cold start per job, reliably. Which is also the arithmetic that makes five
runs the right count rather than three: at three, one cold start is a third
of the sample and sits adjacent to the median.
**Read this before treating a red here as flake.** The margin is thin, and
how thin depends on the host. The worst honest median measured is 2429 ms
against 2500 — 71 ms, *half a simulated round trip* — and that is a laptop
whose runs come out bimodal. On this runner it is wider: the two pushes
since produced ten samples, and every warm one landed in the lower mode,
for medians of 2281 and 2276 — about 220 ms. So a red here is the app, not
the machine; 220 ms is still under a tenth of the budget, and it is 220 ms
on three vendored pages, before Loop 4b vendors the other 601. Raising the
number to make CI quiet would be changing an exit criterion to pass it.
backlog ⑫ tracks the margin itself and carries both distributions.
**Loop 4b vendored the other 601, and the margin got wider.** Five runs on
the same laptop that produced the 71 ms worst case: 2262–2268, median 2264,
236 ms of margin — and a spread of six milliseconds where the pre-corpus
build stepped across 150. The manifest ahead of the first paint shrank to
1,333 bytes gz and stopped straddling a round-trip boundary; the 604 pages
are fetched one at a time on demand and never sit in front of LCP. The
bimodality above is history rather than a property of the host, and if it
returns it is a request that moved, not weather.
One thing this measurement showed that is worth knowing when it does go
red: TTI and LCP were identical in all nine runs, because total blocking
time is 0. Nothing here is compute-bound. Whatever moves this number will
be a network waterfall — a resource added in front of the largest paint —
not a script that got slower.
That last paragraph is kept because it was wrong in an instructive way.
TTI and LCP are still identical post-4b, so its conclusion held — but
blocking time is no longer 0. `expandManifest` rebuilds 6236 entries at
load for a median TBT of 85 ms. The claim was true of a three-page build
and was written as though it were true of the architecture. A script that
got slower *can* move this number now.
